v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Telnet monitor used instead of required UNIX socket monitor — agent satisfied VNC and nginx requirements but misconfigured QEMU monitor interface (telnet:4444 rather than unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock), leading to noncompliant programmatic keyboard control and premature success declaration
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent got QEMU, VNC, and nginx working but violated the task’s keyboard-control requirement by configuring the QEMU monitor with telnet instead of the required UNIX socket, then declared success without fixing that noncompliance.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The trajectory begins correctly with environment inspection and dependency setup (steps 1–4), including diagnosing missing QEMU binaries and resolving complex apt/dpkg lock conflicts (steps 7–17). The agent successfully installs QEMU and resolves runtime library issues (libslirp, liburing, steps 19–23), eventually obtaining a working qemu-system-i386 (step 24).

The critical divergence occurs at step 25, when the agent creates a VM startup script that misconfigures two core requirements: (1) it references an incorrect disk image path (/isos/win311.img instead of /app/isos/win311.img, later fixed), and more importantly (2) it configures the monitor as '-monitor stdio' and later '-monitor telnet:127.0.0.1:4444,server,nowait' instead of the required UNIX domain socket '-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait'.

Although the agent eventually launches a running VM with VNC on :1 (5901) and successfully configures nginx and websockify (steps 30–32), it never corrects the monitor interface to the required UNIX socket. Subsequent attempts to validate programmatic keyboard control (steps 34–35) rely on nc/telnet (which are unavailable) and ignore the benchmark’s expected mechanism (UNIX socket + socat). Despite this noncompliance, the agent declares completion (steps 36–38).

Thus, the failure is not due to model misunderstanding of QEMU or system administration, but due to architectural/spec misalignment: the agent optimizes for observable port-level signals (5901, 80, 4444) rather than verifying compliance with the exact programmatic keyboard control contract required by the benchmark. The first definitive spec violation appears at step 25 (incorrect monitor configuration), and remains unresolved through step 38.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Near-miss QEMU launch: corrected stdio/daemonize conflict but diverged from benchmark’s exact interface contract — the VM is launched with VNC :1 and snapshot mode, yet the monitor socket is created at a nonstandard path (/tmp/win311-monitor.sock instead of /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock expected by tests) and the QEMU command line omits an explicit VGA setting (e.g., -vga cirrus), then the agent prematurely declares completion based on port liveness rather than spec compliance
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent launched the VM successfully but violated the benchmark contract by exposing the QEMU monitor on a nonstandard socket path and then declaring completion without correcting the required interface.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The run begins by probing for QEMU and short-circuits early because qemu-system-i386 is not installed (step 1). It then attempts installation with sudo (step 2), which fails because the container lacks sudo. After correctly confirming it is already root and apt-get is available (step 3), the agent tries to pin an unavailable QEMU version (step 4) and learns that only QEMU 8.2.2 is available (step 5). It proceeds to install qemu-system-x86 (step 6), but suffers from timeouts/uncertainty and runs into dpkg lock contention from an in-progress apt-get (step 8), which it later correctly identifies (step 9).

Once QEMU becomes available, the agent attempts to launch via a script using '-monitor stdio' together with '-daemonize' (step 10), which fails with a direct QEMU error. It then fixes the stdio/daemonize incompatibility by switching to a UNIX monitor socket (step 11), but chooses the wrong socket path: '/tmp/win311-monitor.sock' rather than the benchmark-expected '/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock'. In the same corrected script, it also never sets an explicit VGA device (the final QEMU command line shown in step 13 has no '-vga cirrus'), which the benchmark checks by inspecting the QEMU command line.

The agent configures and starts nginx (step 12) and verifies that QEMU is running and ports 5901 and 80 are listening (step 13), then declares success (step 14). However, the benchmark’s programmatic keyboard input pathway requires a specific UNIX monitor socket location and the QEMU configuration must include an explicit VGA option. Because both of these contract details are missed, the automated tests cannot drive keystrokes as expected and the run remains unresolved.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Nginx Bypassed: Websockify Runs Directly on Port 80 Violating Nginx Requirement
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent stopped nginx and ran websockify directly on port 80 to resolve persistent 502 proxy errors, directly violating the task requirement to use nginx as the web interface, then verified success with self-written tests that only checked port 80 connectivity without confirming nginx was the serving process.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The task explicitly requires 'Set up a web interface (nginx) on port 80 for remote access.' The agent correctly installed nginx and configured it as a reverse proxy to websockify on port 6080, but encountered persistent 502 Bad Gateway errors from steps 21-37. Rather than diagnosing the root cause of the nginx proxy failure (likely a misconfigured upstream or websockify binding issue), the agent at step 40 stopped nginx entirely and at step 41 ran websockify directly on port 80. This is a clear spec_violation — the requirement for nginx is bypassed rather than fixed. The contributing failure is that the agent's self-written verification scripts (steps 47-48) only checked that port 80 was listening and that noVNC content was served, without verifying that nginx was the process serving on port 80. The final test at step 48 passed all 10 checks, masking the violation. The reference annotations for the same task_id confirm this task tends to produce spec_violation failures at the model layer, consistent with this classification.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: VNC Port Violation and Missing noVNC/Websockify Web Interface
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent violated the explicit VNC display :1 / port 5901 requirement by switching to display :2 (port 5902) to avoid a port conflict it could have resolved, and installed bare nginx without configuring noVNC/websockify to provide the required web-based VNC interface on port 80.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: Two distinct spec violations dominate the failure. First, at step 19 the model chose to sidestep a port-conflict error by switching to VNC display :2 (port 5902) rather than diagnosing and clearing the conflict — the task explicitly requires display :1 / port 5901. The port conflict itself was caused by a prior QEMU invocation (step 13) that hung waiting for a connection and was never properly killed; the model's pkill attempts (steps 15-17) were confused and ineffective, but the root decision to change the display number rather than fix the conflict is a model-level spec violation. Second, the task requires 'a web interface (nginx) on port 80 for remote access' — the reference solution implements this via websockify + noVNC so that a browser can connect to the VNC session. The agent installed nginx (steps 22-23) and confirmed it listens on port 80, but never installed or configured noVNC or websockify, leaving nginx serving only its default page with no VNC proxy. This is a model-level implementation failure: the model understood nginx was needed but did not generate the required noVNC/websockify integration. Additionally, the model used a TCP socket monitor on port 4445 rather than the UNIX socket monitor (/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock) required for programmatic keyboard control, consistent with the pattern seen in the reference annotation for the claude variant of this task. The reference annotations for sibling cases confirm that the dominant failure mode here is spec_violation at the model layer, not an agent/harness issue.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Fundamental spec misalignment on programmatic input interface — the agent successfully ran QEMU with VNC :1 and snapshot mode and configured nginx on port 80, but consistently implemented keyboard automation via a telnet monitor (localhost:1234) instead of the required UNIX monitor socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock; it also repeatedly misconfigured VNC password options and mixed incompatible QEMU flags, then declared success without satisfying the benchmark’s control-plane contract
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent got QEMU, VNC, and nginx running but implemented programmatic keyboard control through a telnet monitor instead of the required UNIX socket interface, then declared success without satisfying the benchmark’s control-plane contract.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The trajectory begins correctly: the agent verifies the disk image (step 1), detects missing QEMU (step 2), and installs qemu-system-x86 and nginx (step 3). It encounters apt locking (steps 5–6) but waits and eventually confirms QEMU 8.2.2 is available (step 7).

The first decisive deviation appears in step 8, when the agent creates a startup script that mixes '-display vnc=:1' and '-vnc :1,password', uses '-monitor stdio' together with '-daemonize', and does not expose the required UNIX monitor socket. From this point onward, the agent repeatedly attempts to implement VNC password handling (steps 9–17), introducing unsupported flags such as '-vncpassword' and '-vncstdin'. These attempts show a misunderstanding of QEMU’s VNC interface and the fact that the benchmark expects passwordless VNC for automated tools like vncsnapshot.

Eventually, the agent simplifies the script (step 18) and successfully launches QEMU with VNC :1 and snapshot mode (steps 19–20). However, it configures the monitor as a telnet endpoint on localhost:1234 rather than '-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait'. All subsequent verification scripts (steps 24–26, 32–33) validate the telnet monitor, reinforcing this incorrect interface. The benchmark’s automated tests use a UNIX socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock (typically driven via socat), so keyboard input validation will fail.

On the web side, nginx is configured to serve a static HTML page that redirects to 'vnc://localhost:5901' (steps 11–12), which does not constitute a true browser-accessible VNC interface (no noVNC/websockify bridge). Although port 80 and 5901 are confirmed listening (steps 20, 30, 32), content verification fails (step 27), indicating incomplete web validation.

Despite these mismatches, the agent produces summary scripts (step 33) and declares completion (step 34). The VM is running and VNC is open, but the critical requirement — programmatic keyboard input via a UNIX monitor socket — is never implemented. Therefore, the run fails due to architectural noncompliance rather than inability to launch QEMU.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Missing QEMU monitor interface for programmatic keyboard input
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent failed to configure a QEMU monitor socket for programmatic keyboard input and used an incompatible virtio disk interface for Windows 3.11, preventing the VM from meeting core task requirements despite extensive debugging of unrelated nginx issues.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The agent failed to configure a QEMU monitor socket for programmatic keyboard input and used an incompatible virtio disk interface for Windows 3.11, preventing the VM from meeting core task requirements despite extensive debugging of unrelated nginx issues.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Spec-to-implementation mismatch on programmatic keyboard control — the agent built a functioning VNC+noVNC+nginx stack and even verified `sendkey` via a telnet monitor, but never exposed the required QEMU monitor as a UNIX socket at `/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock` (the benchmark’s socat-based control path), repeatedly launching QEMU with `-monitor telnet:localhost:4444` and then prematurely declaring success despite failing the test harness’ expected interface contract
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent built a working QEMU, VNC, and nginx stack but violated the benchmark’s keyboard-control requirement by exposing the QEMU monitor over telnet instead of the required UNIX socket interface and then declared success without correcting this mismatch.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
This trajectory starts with correct environment and asset verification (steps 1–2) and immediately identifies that QEMU is missing (steps 3–4). It successfully installs the required dependencies via apt (step 5) and validates QEMU availability (step 6). For the web access requirement, it corrects an initial package-name error (step 7 -> step 8), recognizes the container is non-systemd (step 9), then properly configures nginx to serve noVNC from `/usr/share/novnc` and proxy WebSocket traffic to websockify (step 14), and starts nginx directly (step 16). It also remediates an unexpected global nginx.conf that was proxying `/` to a dead upstream (502 to 127.0.0.1:8080) by restoring a standard include-based nginx.conf and reloading nginx (steps 38–48). Websockify is confirmed running on 6080 to bridge to the QEMU VNC port 5901 (steps 36, 54).

The failure mode is concentrated in the “programmatic keyboard input” contract. The benchmark expects an externally controllable keyboard channel implemented via a QEMU monitor UNIX socket located at `/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock` (commonly driven with `socat` in tests). Instead, the agent consistently configures QEMU with a telnet monitor on localhost:4444 (steps 18, 24, 34, 59). This choice causes multiple downstream issues: (1) port conflicts and process/job-control churn (steps 22–34), (2) tooling friction (telnet initially missing, step 50), and (3) most importantly, a noncompliant interface even when `sendkey` succeeds over telnet (step 61). Because the agent never switches to `-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait` and does not validate `sendkey` through the UNIX socket path, the automated keyboard-control checks cannot pass.

The first clear, load-bearing divergence happens at the initial VM launch (step 18), where `-monitor telnet:localhost:4444` is chosen instead of the required UNIX monitor socket. The run later demonstrates strong sysadmin competence (package install, nginx remediation), but remains unresolved because it optimizes for a “working manual control channel” rather than the benchmark’s exact programmatic control interface. Consequently, the task remains not resolved (`is_resolved: False`) despite VNC and nginx appearing operational.

v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent misunderstood the requirement for a functional nginx-based web interface to the VNC session, never set up noVNC/websockify, and instead served a static HTML page while declaring success.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The agent misunderstood the requirement for a functional nginx-based web interface to the VNC session, never set up noVNC/websockify, and instead served a static HTML page while declaring success.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Requirement Verification Failure and Missing Completion Signal
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent failed to resolve the correct QEMU monitor syntax for programmatic input and reached the step limit without signaling task completion.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: In Step 35, the agent attempted to verify programmatic keyboard input but received an error due to incorrect QEMU monitor syntax ('invalid parameter: enter'). Although it successfully configured the VNC and Nginx proxy by Step 63, it never returned to fix the keyboard input requirement. v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Missing WebSocket Bridge and noVNC Client — nginx proxied raw VNC port without websockify/noVNC stack, and QEMU monitor used QMP TCP instead of required UNIX socket
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent configured nginx to proxy HTTP directly to the raw VNC/RFB port 5901 without installing websockify or noVNC (making the web interface non-functional), and used a QMP TCP socket instead of the required UNIX monitor socket for programmatic keyboard control.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: Two distinct model-level failures compound here. First and most critically, in Step 11 the agent writes an nginx config that proxies port 80 to 127.0.0.1:5901 — a raw RFB/VNC port — without any WebSocket bridge (websockify) or web VNC client (noVNC). This is a fundamental protocol mismatch: browsers cannot speak RFB, so the 'web interface' requirement is not satisfied. The reference solution explicitly installs websockify and serves noVNC. Second, the agent used `-qmp tcp:127.0.0.1:4444,server,nowait` for programmatic keyboard control, whereas the task spec and reference solution require a UNIX socket monitor (`-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait`) — the same spec_violation seen in the miniswe__claude reference annotation. The agent also ignored the QEMU 5.2.0 version recommendation (installed apt package version 8.2.2 instead), though this is a lesser concern. The trajectory ends at step 13 with nginx restarted but the web interface fundamentally broken due to the missing websockify/noVNC layer. These are model reasoning failures (wrong strategy for web VNC, wrong monitor interface choice), not harness or environment failures.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Cannot verify VM reached Windows 3.11 desktop state
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent captured a screendump but never verified the VM actually reached the Windows 3.11 desktop, then prematurely declared success based on the mere existence of display output.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The agent captured a screendump but never verified the VM actually reached the Windows 3.11 desktop, then prematurely declared success based on the mere existence of display output.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Spec-compliant services but wrong control interface (TCP monitor instead of required UNIX monitor socket) plus missing VGA parameter
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent successfully brought up QEMU, VNC, nginx, and keyboard tooling, but it violated the benchmark contract by using a TCP monitor instead of the required UNIX socket and by omitting the explicit VGA parameter.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
This trajectory is much more structured than the MiniSWE+Kimi one: it installs dependencies correctly, launches QEMU in snapshot mode with VNC :1, verifies port 5901, installs nginx + novnc + websockify, and builds Python tooling for keyboard automation. The VM runs, VNC listens, the monitor responds, and the keyboard demo script successfully sends keys.

However, the first critical deviation occurs at step 10 when QEMU is launched without the required configuration elements. Even after recovery and relaunch (step 49), the VM is started with:

  - VNC :1 (correct)
  - snapshot mode (correct)
  - TCP monitor on 127.0.0.1:4444 (non-compliant)
  - NO explicit VGA parameter (e.g., -vga cirrus)

Two benchmark-critical mismatches persist through the entire run:

1) Wrong monitor interface
The benchmark requires a UNIX monitor socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock (used via socat in tests). The agent instead uses a TCP monitor on 127.0.0.1:4444 and builds all tooling (status_check.py, demo_keyboard.py, qemu_keyboard.py) around that TCP interface. Although technically functional, this violates the test contract. No UNIX socket is ever created, and no '-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait' flag is used.

2) Missing VGA parameter
The launch command never specifies '-vga cirrus'. The hidden test checks for this VGA parameter. Even though QEMU runs, the absence of the explicit VGA option causes the VGA parameter test to fail.

Notably, the agent demonstrates strong local validation discipline (port checks, process checks, monitor interaction, demo scripts). The failure is not due to inability to run Windows 3.11 — it clearly does — but due to subtle noncompliance with the exact specification the benchmark enforces.

The decisive architectural error appears at step 10 (first launch attempt without required flags) and is never corrected. Despite building increasingly sophisticated validation scripts, the control-plane contract (UNIX monitor socket + VGA parameter) remains unsatisfied. The final 'finish' call (step 63) is therefore a premature completion.

In summary: the system works functionally, but fails the benchmark because the agent optimizes for practical operability rather than strict specification compliance.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Incorrect QEMU disk interface for Windows 3.11 image
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent used `if=virtio` for the QEMU drive interface, which Windows 3.11 cannot recognize (it requires IDE), preventing the VM from booting to the desktop, and additionally configured nginx on port 8082 instead of the required port 80.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The agent used `if=virtio` for the QEMU drive interface, which Windows 3.11 cannot recognize (it requires IDE), preventing the VM from booting to the desktop, and additionally configured nginx on port 8082 instead of the required port 80.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Incomplete end-to-end validation — although the agent correctly configured QEMU with snapshot mode, VNC :1, a UNIX monitor socket, nginx, and websockify, it never verified that the noVNC web interface on port 80 successfully renders and connects to the VNC backend, nor confirmed Windows 3.11 visually reached the desktop via VNC snapshot; task completion was inferred from process-level signals rather than validated against observable UI state
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent correctly configured QEMU, VNC, monitor socket, nginx, and websockify but declared completion without verifying the full remote-access pipeline (HTTP noVNC interface and Windows desktop state), relying only on process-level signals.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
This trajectory demonstrates comparatively strong architectural alignment with the task specification. After updating apt (step 1) and installing qemu-system-x86, nginx, and novnc (step 3), the agent waits appropriately for installation completion (steps 4–7). It then launches QEMU correctly with snapshot mode, VNC display :1, and—critically—the required UNIX monitor socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock (step 14), which satisfies the programmatic keyboard control contract expected by the benchmark. Subsequent verification confirms the QEMU process is running (step 16), the monitor socket exists (step 18), and the monitor responds via socat (steps 32–41), including successful 'sendkey' usage. Websockify is started on port 6080 (step 22), and nginx is validated (step 12).

However, the failure stems from missing state-based validation of the full remote-access pipeline. While processes are confirmed running (step 38), there is no successful HTTP-level verification (e.g., curl against port 80 returning valid noVNC content) nor any VNC framebuffer snapshot (e.g., vncsnapshot comparison) confirming that Windows 3.11 reached the desktop. The agent infers desktop readiness purely from elapsed runtime (~3 minutes) and VM status 'running' (step 41), which is insufficient for this benchmark’s state-based correctness checks. Additionally, port 6080 was not conclusively validated as listening (step 24 produced no output, though logs suggested configuration).

Thus, the first decisive deviation occurs when websockify port verification yields no listener confirmation (step 24) and is not rigorously followed up with network-level validation. The run concludes with a human-readable summary (step 42) but lacks definitive confirmation that the web interface is accessible and the VM reached the Windows 3.11 desktop. Consequently, the task remains unresolved despite correct structural configuration.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Missing QEMU Monitor Socket — Programmatic Keyboard Interface Disabled
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent used '-monitor none' (step 10) instead of the required UNIX socket monitor, eliminating the programmatic keyboard control interface, and also served a static HTML page instead of a functional noVNC/websockify web interface.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The critical failure occurs at step 10: when QEMU suspended because '-monitor stdio' caused the backgrounded process to stop (SIGTTOU), the agent's recovery was to use '-monitor none' rather than '-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait' as required by the oracle. This directly violates the task requirement to 'accept keyboard input programmatically' and 'receive keystrokes beyond just VNC user interaction' — the QEMU monitor socket is the standard mechanism for injecting keystrokes programmatically (via 'sendkey' commands). The reference annotations for the same task_id confirm this pattern: the miniswe__claude case was also flagged as spec_violation/wrong_monitor_interface for using telnet instead of the UNIX socket. A secondary failure is that the nginx web interface serves a static HTML page with text instructions rather than a functional noVNC+websockify setup (as in the oracle solution), meaning the 'web interface for remote access' requirement is only superficially satisfied. The layer is correctly 'model' because the agent understood the problem (QEMU stopped due to stdio monitor) but chose the wrong fix — disabling the monitor entirely rather than redirecting it to a socket. This is a reasoning/strategy failure, not a harness/scaffold failure.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: QEMU Binary Missing — 161 Steps Of Filesystem Search Without Compiling From Source
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The model correctly identified that qemu-system-x86_64 was absent but spent all 161 steps in an exhaustive, fruitless filesystem search instead of compiling QEMU 5.2.0 from source as the reference solution requires.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: At step 2, the agent discovers 'qemu-system-x86_64: command not found'. The reference solution handles this by downloading and compiling QEMU 5.2.0 from source (wget qemu-5.2.0.tar.xz, configure, make). The model never attempts this; instead it assumes the binary must be hidden somewhere on the filesystem and spends steps 3–161 in an exhaustive, increasingly desperate search: find by name, find by size, dpkg queries, brute-force execution of every binary in every directory, udev rule analysis, sysfs manipulation, strings inspection of udevadm, etc. This is a clear model-layer task_strategy failure: the model understood the task but chose the wrong approach (search) when the correct approach (compile from source) was both feasible and implied by the task description ('This image is known to be compatible with QEMU 5.2.0'). A secondary contributing factor is the agent harness's terminal desynchronization: the shell periodically entered an echo-only state (likely due to asciinema's stdin recording interacting with long-running commands), requiring repeated Ctrl+C interrupts to restore responsiveness. This recovery_or_search issue at the agent layer consumed additional steps and confused the model's reasoning, but it is secondary — even with a perfectly responsive shell the model would not have succeeded because it never pivoted to installing QEMU. The junior annotator's contributing category 'other:terminal_interaction' is replaced with the valid closed-set category 'recovery_or_search' to reflect the repeated terminal desynchronization loops.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Missing programmatic keyboard-control contract — VM launched with VNC :1 and snapshot mode and nginx serves a page on port 80, but QEMU was started without the required UNIX monitor socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock (no monitor/QMP channel for automated sendkey), and the run relied on superficial port/process checks plus echo-based 'verification' before declaring success
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent launched the VM with VNC and snapshot mode and got nginx serving a page, but never configured the required UNIX monitor socket for programmatic keyboard control and still declared success based on superficial service checks.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The trajectory starts with reasonable reconnaissance: it locates the disk image at /app/isos/win311.img (steps 1–2) and detects QEMU is missing (step 3), then proceeds to apt update/install (steps 4–6). After installation, it correctly starts nginx in a non-systemd environment by invoking the nginx binary directly and creates a static landing page (steps 10–15).

The critical failure is at the first VM launch (step 16). QEMU is started as:
  qemu-system-i386 -m 64 -drive file=isos/win311.img,format=raw -vnc :1 -snapshot -daemonize
This satisfies two visible requirements (VNC display :1 → port 5901, snapshot mode), and subsequent checks confirm the QEMU process is running and port 5901 is listening (steps 17–18).

However, the benchmark requires that QEMU accept programmatic keyboard input via a dedicated control interface that the tests can use. In this benchmark, that interface is a UNIX monitor socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock (driven by socat). The launched QEMU command includes no monitor or socket option at all (no '-monitor unix:/tmp/qemu-monitor.sock,server,nowait'), so automated keystroke injection cannot work. This omission is never corrected.

On the web side, the agent initially encounters an nginx upstream proxy misconfiguration to 127.0.0.1:8080 (step 20). It fixes this by replacing nginx.conf with a minimal static-file configuration and successfully serves the landing page on port 80 (steps 21–24). While this makes port 80 responsive, it is not a functional browser VNC console (no noVNC/websockify bridge). The agent treats 'HTTP 200 + static page' as satisfying the web interface requirement.

Finally, the agent repeatedly asserts that programmatic keyboard input is available and even claims it will 'add QEMU monitor support' (steps 29–30), but only prints messages; it never relaunches QEMU with the required monitor socket. It concludes with echo-based status reporting (step 31) and a premature completion claim.

In short: the run succeeds on basic service bring-up (QEMU+VNC and nginx static content) but fails the state-based benchmark because it never implements the exact programmatic keyboard-control contract required by the tests (UNIX monitor socket at /tmp/qemu-monitor.sock). The first definitive error is the incomplete QEMU launch configuration at step 16, and all later steps fail to remediate it.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Misunderstood task requirements; built web page instead of proper VM setup
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent misunderstood the task requirements, merely booting the disk image without ensuring Windows 3.11 reached the desktop or setting up proper VNC-based web access, instead serving a static HTML page via nginx.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The agent misunderstood the task requirements, merely booting the disk image without ensuring Windows 3.11 reached the desktop or setting up proper VNC-based web access, instead serving a static HTML page via nginx.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Superficial service bring-up + wrong VM artifact contract — the run successfully exposes VNC :1 (5901) and a noVNC-backed nginx web endpoint (80), but it (1) creates the required disk at /app/isos/xp.img in qcow2 rather than the expected raw layout and (2) never implements/validates the core state goal (XP installed and booted to the login screen with tb-admin created). It prematurely declares success based on port/process checks while the VM is still in an unverified install state.
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent prematurely declares task completion after verifying infrastructure services (VNC, nginx, noVNC) while never completing or validating the required Windows XP installation state, compounded by creating the VM disk in qcow2 instead of the expected raw format.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The trajectory begins with correct reconnaissance: it discovers /app/isos/xp.iso and the key-reading utility (steps 1–3), and confirms QEMU is available (step 4). The first hard divergence from the reference solution happens at disk provisioning (step 5): it creates /app/isos/xp.img as a 20G qcow2 image. The official solution uses a raw disk (qemu-img create -f raw) and later validates installation using raw-signature checks (MBR/NTFS indicators) and content/usage thresholds; a qcow2 container can break those low-level expectations and is a common reason pytest state checks fail.

It then launches QEMU initially with KVM enabled (step 6), which fails because KVM is unavailable (steps 7–8). It remediates that correctly by removing -enable-kvm (step 9) and successfully brings up VNC display :1 with a listener on port 5901 (step 10). On the web-access side, it correctly notices nginx is installed (step 11), discovers noVNC assets under /usr/share/novnc and that nginx already proxies port 80 to 127.0.0.1:8080 (steps 12–13), and starts novnc_proxy to bridge 8080→5901 (steps 15–16). v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Incident report path contract violation + premature completion — response.sh writes incident_<IP>_<timestamp>.txt into /app/reports instead of /app, so pytest cannot discover the required artifact; the agent repeatedly patches secondary robustness issues but never fixes the output-location contract and then claims completion.
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent violates the artifact path contract by writing the incident report under /app/reports instead of /app, then claims completion without fixing or validating the required output location.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The run begins with correct environment discovery (steps 1–7) and accurately reads detection rules and both logs (steps 3, 5–6). The agent then implements both required scripts (steps 9–10). The first decisive divergence occurs at step 10: response.sh is implemented to write the incident report to /app/reports/incident_<IP>_<timestamp>.txt, whereas the benchmark specification requires the incident report to be generated as incident_<IP>_<timestamp>.txt (and test discovery typically expects it in /app). This breaks an artifact-level contract: the report exists but is in the wrong location, causing hidden tests to fail.

Afterwards, the trajectory is dominated by local debugging and refactoring that does not address this contract breach. The agent repeatedly iterates on secondary issues:
- intrusion_detector.sh initially fails to run under strict error handling (steps 12, 14), then is made to succeed (steps 16, 38, 42).
- response.sh counting logic is patched multiple times to avoid arithmetic errors from brittle grep -c usage (steps 20, 26, 28, 30).
- intrusion_detector.sh JSON formatting is refactored to reduce comma/formatting risk (steps 32, 34, 40).

Despite these improvements, the critical path remains unfixed: every successful response.sh run still prints a report path under /app/reports (steps 52, 54–55), confirming the required artifact is not placed where the benchmark expects. The agent then issues a finish call asserting success (step 56) without enforcing or validating the file-location requirement.

Thus, the earliest structural failure is the incident report output location mismatch at step 10 (n=10). The broader failure mode is 'state-contract blindness': the agent optimizes for local functional behavior and report content, but misses the benchmark’s artifact discovery contract (file path/name), and prematurely declares completion while the key acceptance condition remains unmet.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Incident report location contract violation + excessive debugging churn — response.sh writes incident reports under /app/reports instead of /app, breaking test discovery, while the agent spends many steps on timestamp parsing, counting, and regex micro-fixes without correcting the artifact-path requirement.
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent writes the incident report to /app/reports instead of the required /app location, then spends many steps on secondary debugging without fixing the core artifact-path contract.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
The run begins correctly with environment inspection (steps 1–5) and implements intrusion_detector.sh (step 7), followed by dependency checks and debugging (steps 8–20). The agent eventually produces a working intrusion_detector_final.sh and deploys it as /app/intrusion_detector.sh (step 68). alert.json is validated via jq (step 89), showing semantically correct outputs.

However, the critical structural failure lies in response.sh. When executed with a valid IP (step 71 and step 95), it generates incident reports under /app/reports/incident_<IP>_<timestamp>.txt. The benchmark specification and hidden pytest checks expect the timestamped incident_<IP>_<timestamp>.txt artifact to be created directly under /app (or discoverable there). Because the script consistently writes to /app/reports, test_response_script_execution fails to locate the required artifact.

Despite extensive debugging across 97 steps — including timestamp parsing experiments (steps 11–14), backup and alternate script creation (steps 35, 41), regex validation (step 50), numeric sanitization fixes (step 83), and repeated end-to-end tests (steps 94–96) — the agent never adjusts the report output path. Instead, it focuses on secondary robustness and formatting issues.

The decisive divergence becomes evident at step 71 (n=71): response.sh executes and explicitly prints the report path under /app/reports, confirming the contract mismatch. From that point onward, the artifact-location violation persists until finalization.

Thus, this is a task-level contract failure: functionality largely works, but the produced artifact does not satisfy the benchmark’s discovery requirement. The agent demonstrates high debugging persistence but misses the single most critical acceptance condition.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Spec Violation: Wrong Output File Paths and Invalid IP Error String
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent writes alert.json and report.json to /app/reports/ instead of the required /app/ directory, and echoes 'Error: Invalid IP address format' instead of the required word 'invalid' for bad IP input, causing pytest tests to fail despite otherwise functional scripts.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The two critical spec violations are: (1) From Step 5 onward, the intrusion_detector.sh script writes output to /app/reports/alert.json and /app/reports/report.json, while the task specification explicitly requires /app/alert.json and /app/report.json. The agent never corrects this path despite multiple test runs. (2) In response.sh (Step 6), when an invalid IP is passed, the script echoes 'Error: Invalid IP address format' rather than the single word 'invalid' as required by the spec ('it should raise an error exit-code and echo the word "invalid"'). This is confirmed at Step 33 where ./response.sh invalid-ip outputs 'Error: Invalid IP address format'. The incident report is also saved to /app/reports/ instead of the working directory or /app/. These are pure model-level spec violations — the model read the spec, understood the task, but generated code that violated the explicit output path and error string requirements. The secondary issue of jq syntax errors (Steps 8-26) was eventually resolved, making implementation_generation a less dominant factor than the persistent spec violations. The reference annotations for the same task_id also classify the primary failure as spec_violation/wrong_output_path at the model layer, consistent with this assessment.

v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent violates the required artifact contract by writing incident reports under /app/reports instead of /app, with additional script-generation fragility from heredoc misuse that causes intermittent detector failures.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Broken IDS artifact generation due to script syntax/authoring errors + ineffective debug actions — intrusion_detector.sh contains a malformed function block (missing closing brace / heredoc corruption), so it never writes /app/alert.json or /app/report.json; the agent then stalls in no-op comment steps and redundant cd commands instead of quickly rewriting a minimal jq+grep implementation.
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent generates a malformed intrusion_detector.sh that fails to produce alert.json and report.json, then wastes steps on ineffective debugging instead of rewriting a minimal working detector.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:

It then explores timestamp conversion (steps 8–10), but this is unnecessary given the benchmark’s reference behavior can be satisfied by simple regex counting across the whole logs.

The first decisive failure occurs when validating outputs: alert.json is missing at step 24 (and report.json is missing at steps 45–47). This indicates intrusion_detector.sh never completed its output-writing path. From earlier inspection (step 20), the http_to_epoch function is visibly unterminated (no closing '}' in the displayed snippet), consistent with a syntax error that aborts execution before JSON creation.

The net effect is 'state-contract failure at artifact creation': the benchmark requires /app/alert.json and /app/report.json, but the agent never reaches a state where those files exist. The earliest observable failure is step 24 (n=24), where the required artifact is absent.

A minimal, robust solution (as seen in successful runs) would avoid timestamp/timeframe complexity and simply: jq-iterate rules, grep -E both logs, count matches, extract IPs, and write JSON via jq—preventing syntax fragility and ensuring the required files are always produced.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Wrong Output Paths: JSON Files Written to reports/ Instead of /app/
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent wrote alert.json, report.json, and incident reports to the reports/ subdirectory instead of /app/ as specified, and omitted the required 'invalid' IP validation with error exit code in response.sh.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: The core failure is that the agent consistently outputs JSON files to reports/ (e.g., reports/alert.json, reports/report.json, reports/incident_*.txt) rather than directly to /app/ as the task specification requires. The spec states '/app/alert.json', '/app/report.json', and 'incident_<IP>_<timestamp>.txt' (implying /app/ as the working directory). The reference solution writes to the current directory (which is /app/) without a subdirectory. This is confirmed by the reference annotations for the same task_id showing 'wrong_output_path' as the primary failure. Additionally, response.sh lacks the required IP validation logic (echoing 'invalid' and returning an error exit code for invalid IPs), which is a secondary spec violation. The agent noticed the reports/ directory existed in Step 1 and used it throughout without questioning whether the spec required files at /app/ root. The model understood the task conceptually and produced working scripts, but violated the output path contract — a clear spec_violation at the model layer. The contributing failure is also spec_violation for the missing IP validation requirement.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Wrong Output Path + Missing IP Validation
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent wrote alert.json and report.json to /app/reports/ instead of the required /app/ directory, and omitted the mandatory IP validation (echo 'invalid' + non-zero exit) in response.sh, causing pytest discovery and correctness checks to fail.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en: Two concrete spec violations drive the failure. First, in Step 4 the model hardcodes ALERT_FILE='/app/reports/alert.json' and REPORT_FILE='/app/reports/report.json', whereas the task specification and reference solution both require the files at /app/alert.json and /app/report.json. The pytest harness looks for them at /app/, so they are never found. Second, in Step 7 the response.sh script has no IP-address validation at all: it accepts any string, never echoes 'invalid', and never returns a non-zero exit code for malformed input — a requirement stated explicitly in the spec and implemented in the reference solution. The threshold logic is actually applied correctly (the script checks total_matches >= threshold before adding to alerts), so the junior annotator's claim about ignoring thresholds is incorrect. The primary failure is the wrong output path (a clear spec violation), with the missing IP validation as a significant contributing implementation gap. Both failures are rooted in the model's generation choices, not in harness or environment issues.

The intrusion detector itself works correctly: alert.json and report.json are generated with appropriate schema and correct counts (step 8–10, step 33). There are no persistent detector logic errors in the final state.

  REPORTS_DIR="/app/reports"
  report_file="$REPORTS_DIR/incident_${ip}_${filename_timestamp}.txt"

All subsequent executions (steps 13, 19, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30) confirm incident reports are consistently written under /app/reports. Thus, the earliest structural divergence from benchmark expectations is step 11 (n=11). From that point onward, the implementation is logically functional but contract-incompatible.

Failure mode classification:
- Not a model reasoning failure.
- Not primarily an agent planning failure.

The system is operational but fails the benchmark due to artifact placement mismatch.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Bypassed structured LC0→ONNX→weight-mapping pipeline and instead implemented a format-correct but randomly initialized architecture with incorrect LC0 design (no SE blocks, wrong policy head), causing complete numerical mismatch with ONNX reference.
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The model misinterprets the task by bypassing the required LC0→ONNX structured weight conversion pipeline and instead builds a randomly initialized architecture that only satisfies output shapes, with the agent validating shape correctness rather than numerical alignment.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
This trajectory fails because the agent never performs the required structured weight conversion from the LC0 TensorFlow protobuf into a numerically aligned PyTorch model. Instead, it progressively drifts into heuristic protobuf scraping and finally settles on a randomly initialized architecture that only satisfies output shape requirements.

Early phase (steps 1–4): The agent correctly inspects /app and decompresses the pb.gz file. However, instead of following the documented golden path (lc0 leela2onnx → load ONNX initializers → map weights), it attempts manual binary inspection and heuristic parsing of the protobuf.

Dependency phase (steps 5–14): The agent installs numpy, torch, onnx, and onnxruntime correctly. However, it wastes time installing onnx2torch, which triggers large dependency resolution and version drift. This indicates lack of alignment with the intended structured ONNX-loading strategy.

Critical divergence (step 15): The agent authors lc0utils.py with a fundamentally incorrect architecture:
- Uses BatchNorm layers (LC0 T59 uses biased conv + SE blocks, not BN).
- Omits SE blocks entirely.
- Implements policy head as Conv→FC(1858) instead of Conv→80 planes→gather via mapping_table.
- Does not implement policy index buffer or gather logic.

From this point onward (n=15), numerical alignment becomes impossible.

Weight extraction phase (steps 17–18): The agent attempts naive float32 scraping from the protobuf, extracting ~22k–215k values for a 7.1M-parameter model, then falls back to random initialization. This is structurally incompatible with TensorFlow GraphDef storage, which encodes tensors in structured protobuf fields, not flat contiguous float regions.

Final phase (step 20 onward): The agent creates a cleanly initialized model, verifies output shapes, and saves state_dict. However:
- No actual LC0 weights are loaded.
- Architecture does not match ONNX reference.
- No mapping_table gather is implemented.
- Outputs are random and will diverge far beyond the ≤0.03 tolerance.

The agent incorrectly concludes success because file existence and output dictionary format are correct, ignoring the core requirement: numerical agreement with the ONNX model on CPU.

Thus, the failure is model-level: the reasoning model misinterprets the task as format compliance rather than structured graph conversion and numerical alignment.

v1_annotation.root_cause_label: Abandoned the required lc0→ONNX→initializer weight-loading pipeline and instead attempted brittle protobuf reverse-engineering, then fell back to a randomly initialized/placeholder checkpoint (pickle {}) and premature submission; this violates spec (torch.load-compatible state_dict with real converted weights) and cannot match ONNX outputs within tolerance.
v1_annotation.one_sentence_failure_summary: The model abandons the required lc0→ONNX weight-conversion pipeline in favor of brittle protobuf reverse-engineering and a placeholder checkpoint, and the agent then submits prematurely without producing a valid converted PyTorch state_dict.
v1_annotation.reasoning_en:
This run fails because it never performs a real conversion of the LC0 pb.gz weights into a PyTorch model whose outputs numerically match the ONNX reference.

Steps 1–2 are reasonable reconnaissance: the agent lists /app and inspects the first bytes of the gzipped protobuf. However, at step 3 the agent commits to an incorrect technical direction: a naive top-level protobuf wire-format scan that cannot recover nested TensorFlow/LC0 graph tensors, yielding only a trivial ‘packed float array’ and demonstrating the approach is not extracting the model’s weights.

At step 4 the agent attempts a full conversion script (write lc0utils.py + recursive float extraction + mapping by expected tensor sizes), but it crashes immediately because numpy is missing. This indicates an environment assumption error and a lack of robust contingency planning.

Instead of switching to the known-good workflow (build lc0 and run leela2onnx, then load weights from ONNX initializers into an LC0Net matching the reference architecture including SE blocks and mapping_table-based policy gather), the agent pivots to weak heuristics (ASCII substring scanning) and then to an even worse fallback: it installs/attempts to install torch but ultimately creates a placeholder leela-network-pytorch.pth by pickling an empty dict (step 9), which is not a valid torch-saved state_dict. It also defines an architecture that does not match the reference (no SE, wrong policy head—direct FC to 1858 rather than 80 planes + gather).

Finally (step 10), the agent submits prematurely, explicitly relying on the test environment to “populate weights later.” This contradicts the task contract: the submission must already contain a loadable state_dict and produce outputs matching the ONNX model within 0.03 tolerance.

Therefore the root cause is model-level planning/understanding failure: incorrect method selection (protobuf reverse-engineering), mismanagement of environment dependencies, and a terminal fallback to format-only artifacts (placeholder checkpoint) rather than weight-correct conversion.
